841.title: Lohgarh and the Gurus' coins
841.hook: Banda strikes coins and seals in the name of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh
841.tomorrow: Land to those who work it
841.howItsDone: Sikhs remember that Banda Singh Bahadur struck coins and a seal at Lohgarh in the names of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh rather than his own, and the words deg and tegh are still used for the Khalsa's twin duty to feed and to protect.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chappar Chiri: an ending arrived, but couldn't give back what was lost. Your line was it came. Today, something small enough to hold in your palm.

Take a coin out of a pocket or a purse and turn it over. There's usually a name on it, or a face, or a seal: whoever claims the right to say this metal is worth something. A coin says who rules here. So it means something that once Banda Singh held territory, he made his base in the hills at a fort called Lohgarh, and from there he struck coins and stamped seals. The question is whose name went on them.
screen: `TURN A COIN OVER.` → `A NAME SAYS WHO RULES HERE.` → `COINS STRUCK AT LOHGARH.`

segments.voice: Banda Singh now had a fort, an army and lands under his hand. He could have stamped his own name. He didn't. Sikh tradition says the coins and the seal were struck in the names of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh, the first Guru and the tenth. Remember the instructions tradition says came with the five arrows: never set yourself up as a Guru, and remember you serve the Khalsa. The coins look like that instruction made into metal. The power was real, but the name on it belonged to someone else. The words on his seal were in Persian, and as Sikh tradition reads them, they speak of deg and tegh. The deg is the cooking pot, the great kettle of the langar where anyone can eat. The tegh is the sword, raised to protect. Pot and sword, side by side, as the gift of the Gurus: a short summary of what the Khalsa was meant to be. Feed people, and defend them. Some readers hear in these coins the stamp of Sikh rule. Others hear something quieter: a man with every chance to make his own name large chose to stamp the names of his Gurus instead. On an ordinary day the pull is the same in small ways: the report with our name at the top, the credit we'd like to keep. The coins of Lohgarh point the other way.

segments.voice: Hold a coin if one is near, or picture one, and read what's on it slowly: whose name, whose face, whose words. Then ask what name you'd want stamped on the things you make, your work, your kindness, your choices; maybe someone who taught you, maybe Waheguru. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out as you hold it.
Deg tegh, the cooking pot and the sword. The gift of the Gurus, stamped into the seal Banda Singh struck at Lohgarh, in his Gurus' names.
Your line: in their names. The pot and the sword, and someone else's name on both. Until tomorrow.

842.title: Land to those who work it
842.hook: Banda breaks the big estates and gives land to the farmers who tilled it
842.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Banda Singh Bahadur for giving land to the farmers who tilled it, and connect it to Guru Nanak's teaching of kirat karni, earning by honest work, told in the story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago.

segments.voice: Yesterday, coins struck at Lohgarh with the Gurus' names where a ruler's own name would go. Your line was in their names. Today, from coins to soil.

Two people stand at the edge of a field. One has mud to the knees; he plowed it, sowed it, and will cut it at harvest. The other has clean hands and a paper that says the field is his, and when the grain comes in, he takes the larger share. Tradition remembers that in Banda Singh's Punjab, land often worked that way: big landholders collected, and the people who did the work kept what was left. Where Banda Singh's rule reached, tradition says, he turned that around.
screen: `MUD TO THE KNEES.` → `CLEAN HANDS AND A PAPER.` → `BANDA SINGH TURNS IT AROUND.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Banda Singh broke up the big estates in the lands he held and gave the fields to the farmers who actually tilled them. Accounts differ on how far and how long this reached; he held those lands only for a time, under constant attack. The idea is what Sikhs keep, and it is older. Sikh tradition tells of Guru Nanak staying with a carpenter named Bhai Lalo, a poor man who earned his bread by his own hands. A rich official, Malik Bhago, held a great feast and expected the holy man to come. Guru Nanak stayed with Lalo's plain bread. In the story, when the Guru is pressed to explain, he holds Lalo's coarse bread in one hand and Malik Bhago's rich food in the other, and squeezes them. From Lalo's bread comes milk. From the feast, blood, because it was gathered from other people's labor. The Sikh word for that honest labor is kirat. Kirat karni, earning by honest work, is a pillar of Sikh life, taught beside remembering the Name and sharing. Banda Singh's land grants take that story out of a kitchen and into whole villages. The bread belongs with the hands that made it; the field belongs with the hands that work it. Some readers hear a modern echo whenever people argue about who should own the fields they farm. But at its root, the idea is a carpenter's bread, held up against a feast.

segments.voice: Think of the last thing you ate and trace it backward, one step at a time: the shop, the truck, the packing shed, and finally a field somewhere, with a person bent over it in the heat or the cold. You'll never know their name; hold them in mind anyway, and let a simple thank you rise toward them. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out, and remember the hands behind your bread.
Kirat, honest work. Behind Banda Singh's fields for the tillers: Guru Nanak's honor for earning by one's own hands.
Your line: land to the tillers. In the story, honest bread gives milk. Eight hundred forty-two days, and counting.

843.title: Hunted in the hills
843.hook: Mughal armies pursue Banda through the hills for years
843.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Banda Singh Bahadur's years of being pursued through the hills as a time of chardi kala, ever-rising spirits, a phrase that closes the Ardas said at Sikh gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a carpenter's bread and fields given to the hands that worked them. Your line was land to the tillers. Today the tide turns, and the hunt begins.

Night at Lohgarh. The fort in the hills is surrounded. The emperor's army has come north in force, and the walls won't hold much longer. Inside, tradition says, one Sikh makes an offer. He'll put on Banda Singh's clothes and sit where Banda Singh sits, so that when the enemy breaks in, they'll think they have their man. In the dark, the real Banda Singh slips out through the hills with whoever can follow. By morning the fort has fallen, and the man they capture isn't the one they came for.
screen: `LOHGARH IS SURROUNDED.` → `A SIKH WEARS BANDA SINGH'S CLOTHES.` → `OUT INTO THE HILLS BY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: That night begins a long stretch of Banda Singh's life with no grand battles to name it. The Mughal armies kept after him, season after season, through the hills and the jungles at the edge of the plains. He'd vanish, regroup, strike, and vanish again. Lands won were lost. Towns changed hands. The people who sheltered his men paid a price. Sikh tellings don't make this part glamorous: cold camps, short food, running at night, the slow grind of being hunted. What kept them going? Sikhs have a phrase for it that appears at the end of the Ardas, the prayer said at the close of Sikh gatherings: chardi kala. It means something like rising spirits, an ever-ascending spirit. Not cheerfulness, and not pretending things are fine. Chardi kala is the steadiness to keep facing upward when every report is bad. In the Ardas it's paired with a wish for the good of all, which says something about where that spirit is meant to point. And notice the man who wore Banda Singh's clothes. Earlier on this path, at Chamkaur, tradition told of a Sikh named Sangat Singh who wore the Guru's plume so the Guru could slip away. Now it happens again. That pattern is its own kind of chardi kala: a willingness to stand in someone else's place so the work can keep going. The hills didn't change the hard news. But one borrowed set of clothes bought one night, and one night was enough to keep going.

segments.voice: Name, quietly, the thing in your week that feels like being hunted: the deadline, the bill, the worry that keeps finding you, and don't fight it. Then find one small next step, the size of one night's walk in the hills, not the whole road, and rest your attention on that step and on your breathing. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out, and let the words chardi kala sit beside it.
Chardi kala, rising spirits. The steadiness Banda Singh and his men kept through the long hunt in the hills and jungles after Lohgarh fell.
Your line: keep going. One night at a time still counts as going. Day eight hundred forty-three, done.

844.title: The siege of Gurdas Nangal, 1715
844.hook: starved in a mud fort for months, Banda's men are finally captured
844.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the siege of Gurdas Nangal, where Banda Singh Bahadur and his companions were starved until they were captured, as an example of sidak, steadfast faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a disguise at Lohgarh and a long hunt through the hills. Your line was keep going. Today the hunt narrows to one walled place. Go gently with this one.

Mud walls. Not stone, not a fortress on a cliff. A walled compound in a village called Gurdas Nangal, with a ditch around it, and inside, Banda Singh and his people: fighters, and with them families. Outside, an army settles in to wait. Nobody storms the walls. They don't need to. They simply make sure nothing comes in: no grain, no supplies. Tradition says the waiting went on for months.
screen: `MUD WALLS AND A DITCH.` → `AN ARMY SETTLES IN TO WAIT.` → `NOTHING COMES IN.`

segments.voice: A siege like this is fought with time and hunger. Sikh tellings describe what happened inside the walls as the food ran out. People ate what grain was left, then the animals, then leaves and grass and the bark of trees. Some tellings go further, and they're hard to hear: people too weak to stand, still keeping their places. Accounts differ on the very end, whether the gate was opened at last, or the army simply walked in on people who could no longer resist. Either way, when hunger had done its work, Banda Singh and the men who were left were taken, worn to almost nothing. The line is they held on. Not they won. Not they escaped. Sikhs have a word for this: sidak. It means steadfastness, a faith that stays fixed when everything around it gives way. It isn't the same as courage in a charge. Courage can be a single moment. Sidak is a long thing: what's left on yet another hungry morning, when nothing heroic is happening and nobody is watching. In Sikh memory, Gurdas Nangal is one of the places where that word was tested hardest. There's a quieter lesson in it too, for a listener whose week has nothing to do with sieges. Much of holding on looks like nothing. It's not leaving. It's getting up again. It's staying where you said you'd stay. That kind of faithfulness doesn't make a good painting, which is maybe why it's worth a word of its own.

segments.voice: Notice your stomach right now: full, empty, somewhere between. Then let your mind rest gently on people who are hungry today, near you or far away, who didn't choose it, and keep them company in your attention without pushing for a feeling. After a while, come back to the people inside those mud walls and to the word sidak, and if you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
Sidak, steadfastness. The long siege in which Banda Singh and his people were starved in a walled compound at Gurdas Nangal until they were captured.
Your line: they held on. Sidak is a long thing, not a single moment. Rest gently tonight.

845.title: The march to Delhi, 1716
845.hook: hundreds of Sikhs are paraded and executed daily, and tradition says none renounced their faith
845.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the captives taken to Delhi with Banda Singh Bahadur, of whom tradition says none gave up their faith, and the Ardas remembers those who kept their sikhi to their last breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mud walls at Gurdas Nangal, and the long faithfulness called sidak. Your line was they held on. Today is a hard day on this path, so take it slowly.

A road from Punjab to the capital, and a procession on it that was meant to be seen. The captives from Gurdas Nangal, Banda Singh among them, were taken to Delhi and paraded through the streets in chains, before crowds. The empire wanted everyone watching to understand what happened to people who rose against it. Then came the executions, a group at a time, day after day. And tradition says every one of the captives was offered the same way out.
screen: `A PROCESSION MEANT TO BE SEEN.` → `PARADED, CHAINED, THROUGH DELHI.` → `THE SAME WAY OUT, OFFERED TO EACH.`

segments.voice: The way out was simple. Give up your faith, and live. Tradition says the offer was made, and that not one of them took it. That's the line: none renounced. Sikhs still tell one story from those days. A mother, tradition says, went to the officials and pleaded for her young son. He isn't really a Sikh, she told them; he was caught up with the others by mistake. And she was granted his release. But when the order reached him, the young man refused it. He said, in the telling, that his mother was mistaken: he was a Sikh, and he would stay with his companions. And he died with them. It's a hard story, and Sikhs don't tell it to make anyone want to die. They tell it for what it shows about faith that's chosen, not inherited or assumed. He could have walked out, and nobody would have blamed him. He decided who he was out loud, at the worst possible moment. There's a Sikh word for the whole of that life: sikhi. The Ardas remembers those who kept their sikhi to their last breath, with their hair uncut, which for a Sikh is part of keeping faith whole. The march to Delhi is part of that memory. Today asks nothing heroic of you. But it leaves a quiet question behind: when it costs something small, a raised eyebrow, an awkward pause, do you say who you are, or let someone else say it for you?

segments.voice: Sit upright, the way people stand when a name is read aloud, and hold in silence the people who were offered a way out and kept their faith instead; if faces come, let them be faces you'll never know. When your mind wanders, return to the silence, as if you stood in a crowd that has gone quiet. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
Sikhi, the Sikh way of life. The captives from Gurdas Nangal, paraded through Delhi and executed day after day, of whom tradition says none renounced it.
Your line: none renounced. Sikhi kept whole: a faith chosen, not just inherited. See you tomorrow.

846.title: Banda's end
846.hook: Banda is tortured and killed in Delhi, with his young son
846.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Banda Singh Bahadur's death in Delhi, with his young son Ajai Singh, as a martyrdom, and honor him by the name Bahadur, the brave.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the captives in Delhi, offered their lives if they would give up their faith. Your line was none renounced. Today the story of Banda Singh reaches its last day. Go gently.

A cot by a river at Nanded. A hermit hurries home, finds a stranger sitting where no one sits, and ends the day calling himself that stranger's banda, his servant. On this path that was only nine days ago; in the story, it's years. The servant carried five arrows north, took towns, struck coins in his Gurus' names, gave fields to farmers, ran through the hills, starved behind mud walls, and was marched in chains to Delhi. Now his companions are gone, and his own turn has come.
screen: `A COT BY A RIVER AT NANDED.` → `FROM SERVANT TO PRISONER.` → `HIS OWN TURN COMES.`

segments.voice: Sikh tellings of Banda Singh's last day are hard, and they don't need to be told in full to be understood. He was brought out in Delhi with his young son, Ajai Singh. Tradition says he was offered his life, as the others were, if he would give up his faith, and he refused. Then the hardest part of the telling: tradition says his little boy was killed in front of him, and that Banda Singh did not break. Then he himself was put to death, slowly, by torture. The tellings dwell less on the pain than on his stillness. Some say an official asked him how a man who had done so much could come to this, and that he answered calmly, speaking of God's will and of how wrongdoers are punished in God's time. The exact words vary, and it's best not to put new ones in his mouth. That's the line: he did not break. Not that he wasn't hurt, or wasn't afraid. Only that what he'd chosen at that cot by the river stayed chosen to the end. Sikhs remember him by the fuller name, Banda Singh Bahadur, the brave. They remember him in more than one way, too; parts of his story were argued over by Sikhs who came after, and that's a story for tomorrow. But on this day the memory is simple. The man who began by calling himself a servant ended as one, keeping faith with the One he served.

847.title: Two Khalsas, one decision
847.hook: tradition says a split among Sikhs was settled by Bhai Mani Singh casting two slips into the Amritsar pool
847.howItsDone: Sikhs greet each other with "Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh," and tell the story of the two slips at Amritsar as part of the history of the Panth after Banda Singh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Banda's end, and your line, he did not break. This week walked from coins struck in the Gurus' names to land for the tillers, the hills, the siege, the march, and the end.

Two slips of paper, folded small. A pool of still water. A crowd on the steps, everyone watching the surface. That, tradition says, is how a bitter argument among Sikhs was settled: not by a vote, not by a fight, but by two pieces of paper and a wait. After Banda Singh, Sikhs split over customs some of his followers had taken up. Both called themselves Khalsa. Both came to Amritsar.
screen: `TWO SLIPS. ONE POOL.` → `NOT A VOTE. NOT A FIGHT.` → `BOTH CALLED THEMSELVES KHALSA.`

segments.voice: As tradition tells it, some of Banda Singh's followers had taken up new customs, including a new greeting. Others held that the Guru had given the Khalsa its greeting already, and that nothing should be added. One side came to be called the Bandai Khalsa. The other called itself the Tat Khalsa, the true or essential Khalsa. Both had fought and suffered. And when they gathered at Amritsar, the tension was close to breaking into violence. So Bhai Mani Singh, the respected Sikh caring for the Harmandir, proposed a test that neither side could rig. Tradition says he wrote two greetings on two slips of paper. On one, the greeting the Bandai Sikhs had taken up. On the other, the greeting the Khalsa had used since Guru Gobind Singh, the one this path heard again on the day of Chappar Chiri: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh. Both slips went into the pool together; whichever floated would be accepted, and everyone agreed to the terms before the slips touched the water. The story says the other slip sank, the Guru's greeting floated, and the matter was settled. Some tellings add more, a wrestling match or a later dispute. But the heart is the same in each: before the outcome, both sides agreed on how they would decide. A fair process is a gift to the side that loses. It lets them walk away without being humiliated, and it lets the community stay one community. Sikhs still greet each other with those words, and the tradition remembers the day a pool of water kept a family from breaking apart.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one disagreement that is still open, at home or at work, and don't decide who's right. Instead, ask what fair way of deciding both of you could agree to before you knew the answer: take turns, ask someone neutral, wait a day. Let it take shape, and if you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
